lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you learnt a powerful little word for kind self-talk. Which word? ('Yet', as in 'I can't do it yet.') Today: resilience, and how to bounce back after a setback.
Resilience is bouncing back after a setback: a lost match, a poor mark, a falling-out. It is not something you either have or don't. It is a set of skills you can build, like a muscle.
A setback is information. What went wrong? What went right? What will I try next? Mistakes help the brain learn, and nearly everyone who is good at something has had many of them.
There are three thinking traps after a setback. Forever: 'I'll never get this.' Everything: 'I'm bad at everything.' All me: 'It's all my fault.' Swap each one for a fairer thought.
Review it in two parts: what went well, and even better if. 'My passes were accurate; even better if I talk to my team more.' Then choose one thing to practise.
The bounce-back steps: notice the feeling, calm your body, look at what happened, plan one next step, then try again. Ask friends, family, teachers or coaches for support: that is a strength.
Wilma Rudolph had polio as a child and wore a leg brace. She trained for years, and in 1960 won three Olympic gold medals in sprinting. Setbacks were part of her story, not the end of it.

Try it in the world: after a setback, write what went well and one even better if. In LIFE, the Goal Board helps you bounce back, and Success Stories tells of people who kept trying. Next: respect online.

exercises.prompt: Resilience is a skill you can build, not something you are born with or without.
exercises.explain: True: like a muscle, resilience grows with practice and support.

exercises.prompt: Which trap is this thought: 'I'll never be good at maths'?
exercises.hint: Does it talk about time, all of life, or blame?
exercises.explain: 'Never' says it will last for ever: the forever trap. Fairer: 'Maths is hard right now; practice helps.'

exercises.prompt: Match each trap to a fairer thought.
exercises.hint: Each fairer thought answers its trap: time, all of life, or blame.
exercises.explain: Never becomes yet; everything becomes this one thing; all my fault becomes we all played a part.

exercises.prompt: After a setback, what is the first bounce-back step?
exercises.hint: Feelings come before thinking and doing.
exercises.explain: First notice the feeling; then calm your body, look at what happened, plan, and try again.

exercises.prompt: What went well, or even better if?
items: I kept trying to the end
exercises.hint: One is something you did; the other is a change for next time.
exercises.explain: Went well: warming up, trying to the end, asking early. Even better if: revising sooner, checking answers.

exercises.prompt: Put the bounce-back steps in order.
exercises.hint: Feelings first, then thinking, then doing.
exercises.explain: Notice, calm, look, plan, try again: the same steps work after any setback.

exercises.prompt: Bram's model bridge collapsed in the test. What is the most resilient next step?
choices: find where it broke and strengthen it
exercises.hint: Which step learns from what happened?
exercises.explain: Finding the weak point turns the setback into information for a stronger bridge next time.

exercises.prompt: Asking for help after a setback is a sign of weakness.
exercises.explain: False: asking friends, family, teachers or coaches for support is a strength and speeds up bouncing back.

exercises.prompt: Which is a fairer thought instead of 'We lost because of me'?
choices: we all made mistakes, and they played well
exercises.explain: A match has many players and two teams: the fair thought shares the reasons.

exercises.prompt: Wilma Rudolph won three Olympic gold medals in 1960. How many years ago was that from 2030?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.

exercises.prompt: Match each setback to a resilient next step.
matches: calm down, then talk it through
ask the coach what to work on
exercises.hint: For each, what step learns and moves forward?
exercises.explain: Team: ask for feedback. Test: practise what you missed. Falling-out: calm down, then talk.

exercises.prompt: Which review is the most useful after a lost match?
choices: one thing that went well and one to improve
the referee lost it for us
exercises.hint: A useful review is honest and leads to practice.
exercises.explain: Naming one strength and one even better if is honest and kind, and it gives one clear thing to practise next week; blaming others, or forgetting it, teaches nothing.

exercises.prompt: Thinking 'this one thing went badly' instead of 'I'm bad at everything' helps you bounce back faster.
exercises.hint: Which thought leaves room to fix one thing?
exercises.explain: True: 'this one thing went badly' keeps the setback small and specific, so you can work on that one thing. 'I'm bad at everything' spreads it to all of life and makes trying again feel pointless.

exercises.prompt: Zara's science test went badly. Put her plan in order.
items: ask the teacher to check her work
calm down and talk to a friend
exercises.hint: Feelings, then facts, then practice, then check.
exercises.explain: Calm down, find what she missed, practise it, ask for feedback, then try again with a practice test.

exercises.prompt: What does Wilma Rudolph's story show about setbacks?
choices: they can be part of the story, not the end
exercises.hint: Think about what happened between the leg brace and the medals.
exercises.explain: Polio as a child and years in a leg brace, then years of training, led to three Olympic gold medals in 1960. Her setbacks were part of her story, not the end of it: practice and support turned them round.

exercises.prompt: A trap, or a resilient thought?
items: I lost today; next time can be different
exercises.explain: Traps: 'always' (forever), 'whole week' (everything) and 'all my fault' (all me). Resilient: 'today' keeps it for now, and 'yet' says you are still learning.
